A firm maintains partners’ capital accounts under the fixed capital method. Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Interest on capital
(B) Partner’s drawings
(C) Additional capital introduced

(I) Credit side of Partner’s Capital Account
(II) Credit side of Partner’s Current Account
(III) Debit side of Partner’s Current Account

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
candidate.explanation: Under the fixed capital method, items such as interest on capital and share of profit are credited to the Partner’s Current Account, while drawings are debited to it. Additional capital introduced is credited to the Partner’s Capital Account.

B misplaces drawings and additional capital; C reverses the interest-on-capital and drawings sides; D misplaces additional capital and share of profit.

are: (i) fixed capital method, and (ii) fluctuating capital method. candidate.body: A company forfeited some fully called-up equity shares of ₹10 each. The holders had not paid the final call of ₹3 per share, but the issue premium of ₹2 per share had been received in full. The total amount credited to Share Forfeiture Account on forfeiture was ₹4,200. How many shares were forfeited?
candidate.explanation: The Share Forfeiture Account is credited with the amount received towards share capital; the premium received is excluded. The amount received towards share capital per share was ₹10 − ₹3 = ₹7. Therefore, the number of shares forfeited was ₹4,200 ÷ ₹7 = 600.

reasons: ₹10 per share is called up, and ₹3 is unpaid, so ₹7 per share of share capital was received. Because the ₹2 premium was received in full, it is not debited on forfeiture; the forfeiture credit therefore excludes it and is ₹7 per share. ₹4,200 ÷ ₹7 = 600 shares (B).

The premium-received condition removes ambiguity: there is no premium amount to reverse. The numerical variant applies the forfeiture-account treatment to a calculation, rather than merely rewording the anchor’s matching question.

Match List-I with List-II.

List-I
(A) Calls in arrears
(B) Calls in advance
(C) Securities premium
(D) Reserve capital

List-II
(I) Amount received over and above the nominal value of shares
(II) Amount called on shares but not received
(III) Called at the time of winding up
(IV) Amount received from a shareholder before it becomes due

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
candidate.explanation: Calls in arrears are amounts called on shares but not received, while calls in advance are received before they are due. Securities premium is the amount received above the nominal value of shares. Reserve capital is called at the time of winding up. Thus, the correct matching is (A)–(II), (B)–(IV), (C)–(I), and (D)–(III).

reasons: The matches are (A)–(II): calls in arrears are called amounts not received; (B)–(IV): calls in advance are amounts paid before due; (C)–(I): securities premium is the amount above nominal value; and (D)–(III): reserve capital is called at winding up. These pairings appear together only in option D.
The other options misassign at least one of calls in advance, securities premium, or reserve capital.

66 Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements Calls in Arrears: Sometimes, the full amount called on allotment and/or call (calls) is not received from the allottees/shareholders. The amount not so received are cumulatively called ‘Unpaid calls’ or ‘Calls in Arrears’. However, it is not mandatory for a company to maintain a separate Calls-in-Arrears Account. There are also instances where some shareholders consider it discreet to pay a part or whole of the amount not yet called-up on the shares allotted to them. Any amount paid by a shareholder in the excess of the amount due from him on allotment/call (calls) is

known as ‘Calls in Advance’ for which a separate account is maintained. A company has the power to charge interest on calls in arrears and is under an obligation to pay interest on calls-in-advance if it accepts them in accordance with the provisions of Articles of Association. Over Subscription: It is possible for the shares of some companies to be over subscribed which means that applications for more shares are received than the number offered for subscription. If the amount of minimum subscription is not received to the extent of 90%, the issue dissolves. In case the applications received are less than the number of shares offered to the

public, the issue is termed as ‘under subscribed’. supporting_spans.quote: 66 Accountancy : Company Accounts and Analysis of Financial Statements Calls in Arrears: Sometimes, the full amount called on allotment and/or call (calls) is not received from the allottees/shareholders. The amount not so received are cumulatively called ‘Unpaid calls’ or ‘Calls in Arrears’. However, it is not mandatory for a company to maintain a separate Calls-in-Arrears Account. There are also instances where some shareholders consider it discreet to pay a part or whole of the amount not yet called-up on the shares allotted to them. Any amount paid by a shareholder in the excess of the amount due from him on allotment/call (calls) is

known as ‘Calls in Advance’ for which a separate account is maintained. A company has the power to charge interest on calls in arrears and is under an obligation to pay interest on calls-in-advance if it accepts them in accordance with the provisions of Articles of Association. Over Subscription: It is possible for the shares of some companies to be over subscribed which means that applications for more shares are received than the number offered for subscription. If the amount of minimum subscription is not received to the extent of 90%, the issue dissolves. In case the applications received are less than the number of shares offered to the

public, the issue is termed as ‘under subscribed’. Issue of Shares at Premium: Irrespective of the fact that shares have been issued for consideration other than cash, they can be issued either at par or at premium. The issue of shares at par implies that the shares have been issued for an amount exactly equal to their face or nominal value. In case shares are issued at a premium, i.e. at an amount more than the nominal or par value of shares, the amount of premium is credited to a separate account called ‘Securities Premium Reserve Account’, the use of which is strictly regulated by law. candidate.body: A firm maintains partners’ accounts under the fixed capital method. After all appropriations, a residual profit of ₹1,20,000 is to be shared equally between its two partners. Which journal entry records the transfer of this profit to the partners?
options: Debit Profit and Loss Appropriation Account ₹1,20,000; credit each partner’s Current Account ₹60,000.
Debit each partner’s Current Account ₹60,000; credit Profit and Loss Appropriation Account ₹1,20,000.
Debit Profit and Loss Account ₹1,20,000; credit each partner’s Current Account ₹60,000.
Debit Profit and Loss Appropriation Account ₹1,20,000; credit each partner’s Capital Account ₹60,000.
candidate.explanation: The residual profit is transferred by debiting the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account and crediting the partners’ accounts in their profit-sharing proportions. Since the partners share equally, each receives ₹60,000. Under the fixed capital method, this credit is recorded in each partner’s Current Account, not Capital Account.

All items like share of profit or loss, interest on capital, drawings, interest on drawings, etc. are recorded in a separate accounts, called Partner’s Current Account. The partners’

capital accounts will always show a credit balance, which shall remain the same (fixed) year after year unless there is any addition or withdrawal of capital. Match each situation in List-I with the appropriate accounting treatment or classification in List-II.

| List-I | List-II |

| (C) Shares are issued for more than their nominal value | (III) Unpaid calls, also called calls in arrears |
| (D) The company resolves that a part of its uncalled capital will be called only if it is wound up | (IV) Amount credited to Securities Premium Reserve |

candidate.explanation: An amount called but not received is unpaid calls, also called calls in arrears. Higher turnover ratio means better utilisation of assets and signifies improved efficiency and profitability, and as such are known as efficiency ratios. assets Turnover; and 6. The formula for its calculation is as follows: Inventory Turnover Ratio = Cost of Revenue from Operations / Average Inventory Where average inventory refers to arithmetic average of opening and closing inventory, and the cost of revenue from operations means revenue from operations less gross profit. Significance : It studies the

Low turnover of inventory may be due to bad buying, obsolete inventory, etc., and is a danger signal.
